Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 326 Aerial Ungulate Survey for Moose (2019-2020) 
 
Background 
An aerial ungulate survey for moose was conducted in January 2020 in Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 326 
using transect survey methodology. This WMU is 1046 km 2 and is located in the Lower Foothills Natural Region of 
west central Alberta. WMU 326 is located south of the North Saskatchewan River, west of the Clearwater River, 
and east of the Ram River. The southern area borders Seven Mile Flats, and Rocky Mountain House is located 
northeast of the WMU. The dominant land-cover is dense conifer forest making wildlife sighting challenging.  
Cut-blocks comprise about 35% of the unit. 
 
The last aerial ungulate survey occurred in February 2010 using a random stratified block methodology. Table 1 
shows the previous year’s population and density estimates for moose.  
 
During the 2020 aerial survey, we recorded sightings of white-tailed deer and mule deer however, the numbers 
observed were too low to provide a reliable estimate. No elk were observed. Feral horse observations and 
locations were also recorded. All of these above observations have been entered into the Fisheries and Wildlife 
Management Information System (FWMIS) at the completion of the survey.  
 
The antlered moose archery only season runs from August 25 - September 23, and the general (rifle) season runs 
from September 24 - October 31 (early season) and November 1-30 (late season). Both the archery only and the 
general (rifle) require Special Licences obtained through the Special Licence application process. There is no 
antlerless moose season in WMU 326. The five-year average hunter success for antlered moose is approximately 
35% (range 25-50%). 
 
The objectives of this survey were to assess the status of moose populations in WMU 326, to determine a 
population estimate based on density estimates, and a population split for sex and age classes. 
 
Survey method 
The transect survey was conducted flying east-west lines at 1.6 km (1 mile) intervals, with 25% coverage (400 m 
wide survey strip) from Jan 22-23, 2020. We flew a total of 10.4 hours under generally fair survey conditions.  
Temperatures ranged from -5 to +5 degrees Celsius with <5-20 km/h winds, and some steep slopes bare of snow. 
 
At each observation point, we counted moose and we determined sex and age and verified that each observation 
was within the transect width. For white-tailed deer and mule deer, we classified each observation for sex and age 
class, but did not record antler size. For feral horses, we counted each observation but did not classify by age.  
 
Because transects varied in length (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969), we calculated the average density (R; #/km 2) of 
moose by summing the total animals counted per transect (Σx) by total area searched (length of transects 
multiplied by 400 m survey strip [Σz]). For a population estimate (unequal sized units, sampl ing without 
replacement), we multiplied the average density (R) by the overall area of the WMU (Z). No correction factor was 
applied for moose population estimates. We calculated the width of the 90% confidence interval by multiplying the t 
statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without 
replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq root variance, and variance=N*(N -n)/(n*(n-1))*(Σx2+R2*Σz2-
2*R*Σxz) with N as the total number of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as the number of transects 
sampled.

Results 
We surveyed 28 transects from Jan 22-23, 2020 for a total survey effort of 603.9 km of transects with an area of 
970 km2. In total, we counted 35 moose from 22 groups; only one moose was unclassified. Of the 34 classified 
moose, 13 (38%) were bulls, 12 (35%) were cows, and 9 (27%) were calves. The bull: cow and calf: cow ratios 
were 1.08 and 0.75, respectively. These ratios are artificially high due to the small numbers of total moose and 
cows observed. 
 
The final density estimate was 0.14/km2 with a 90% confidence interval of 0.07/km 2 to 0.20 km2. The estimated 
moose abundance is 141 (75, 206) in 2020 compared with 417 (316, 518). Note that abundance estimates do not 
overlap between years (high of 202 in 2020 vs. low of 316 in 2010; Table 1).  
 
Due to the majority of the unit being comprised of dense conifer, detecting moose from the air can be challenging 
regardless of survey method. While the different survey methods (transect vs. random stratified block) may 
partially explain the change in moose numbers observed, the marked decline in moose populations is a concern.  
 
In addition to the moose counted within the transect boundaries, an additional 6 moose were observed and 
classified outside the transect boundaries (one in adjacent WMU 320) These additional observations were 
recorded and entered into FWMIS but were not used for calculating population estimate and sex ratios.  
 
A total of 16 wild / feral horses and 11 deer (4 mule, 5 white-tailed and 2 unknown species) were also seen over 
the two days of the survey. 
 
Table 1. Previous density, and age/sex composition ratios for moose in WMUs 326. Survey types have 
included random stratified block (RSB), and transect sampling methods. 
Survey Year Survey Type Population Estimate Moose / km2 +/-% Bull:Cow:Calf 
2005  RSB  300  0.29  unknown  unknown  
2010  RSB  417  0.40  24  80:100:13  
2020  Transect  141  0.14  66  108:100:75
